newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Products Outlook - Diffs seen holding ranges.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Products Outlook - Diffs seen holding ranges.

text.p: U.S. spot refined product differentials will likely remain in a range this week since supply and demand are in balance and underlying NYMEX futures markets appear to be rangebound, traders said.
"Refinery runs have been high everywhere but demand is likely to be good into July," said a Midcontinent trader, referring to unleaded gasoline.
Players said products differentials are only likely to move in the short-term if there is a refinery snag or a sharp swing in the price of crude oil.
Any sharp move in crude oil, however, is not expected by some floor traders at least until the the end of next week's OPEC meeting in Vienna.

On the U.S. Gulf Coast, heating oil for prompt delivery on the Colonial Pipeline was also expected to stay steady. It was offered at 2.25 cents below July NYMEX futures on Monday, unchanged from Friday.
"There's no excitement at all. Nothing will happen until buyers hit their tank tops -- when they can't store any more," one Gulf Coast distillate trader said.

He noted that the contango on NYMEX heating oil -- with September barrels priced 1.30 cents higher than July material -- was encouraging stockbuilding by guaranteeing enough profit to pay storage costs.
"But there's only so much demand for heating oil this time of year," he said.
He added that Colonial Pipeline tariff reductions for northbound shipments of heating oil and premium gasoline were also lending support to differentials.
Gulf low sulfur diesel for prompt delivery was meanwhile, firmed a trace to 1.50 cents under the July print for material, amid talk of European inquiries about two Gulf Coast cargoes.
The differentials may also gain some strength later this week from the start of the wheat harvest in the Oklahoma and Texas region, players said.
"The harvest will mostly affect the Gulf in the beginning but it will move north and we will see more demand for diesel," said a Midcontinent-based low sulphur trader.

On Monday, Group Three low sulphur differentials were pegged unchanged from Friday at 3.75/4.00 cents over the print. The differential is about a penny above year-ago levels because of delays earlier in the year on the Explorer Pipeline that put a squeeze on prompt values.
"Low sulphur is very firm already. Incremental barrels are already hard to come by," said a Midcontinent trader.
U.S. cargo markets should remain thin this week, one East Coast player said, with very few barrels expected on offer due to tightness in the arbitrage market.
"There's no new pickings around," the trader said. "There's very little that has not already been well-known around the market," the trader added.
The arbitrage window between Europe and the U.S. Atlantic Coast sat about $12 a barrel Monday, $10 below the level necessary to make the cross-Atlantic trade profitable.

One Venezuelan gasoline cargo is set for delivery into Boston late Monday or early Tuesday, a Eurograde gasoline cargo has been taken into another refiner's blending program and one European conventional M2 gasoline cargo is set for delivery near June 25.
